stories.headline: Update: Russian Missiles Kill Nine in Kyiv as Ukraine Sinks Russian Ship in Black Sea
stories.summary:
At least nine people were killed and dozens more injured when Russian ballistic missiles struck residential areas across Kyiv on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced. Strikes hit multiple city districts, partially destroying apartment buildings and triggering fires and power outages. A missile also landed near the Lithuanian embassy, shattering windows and scattering debris in the compound.

Separately, Ukrainian drones sank a 100,000-tonne Russian-owned container ship, the Yanina, in the Black Sea roughly 130 miles from Novorossiysk. State-owned Russian nuclear operator Rosatom, which owned the vessel, confirmed the attack and said all 17 crew members were rescued. Rosatom's CEO called the strike "piracy and robbery" and said the ship was carrying civilian cargo including frozen food and construction materials.

The Kyiv strikes come two days after a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Polish territory during a separate mass attack that killed at least eight Ukrainians. Zelensky has urgently appealed for more Patriot air defense interceptors, saying they are the only weapon capable of downing ballistic missiles. He met President Trump in Washington earlier this week to press the case.

Trump, speaking at Camp David on Friday, said the U.S. had not agreed to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot missiles domestically but that talks were continuing, calling it "a big step" that required caution. Ukraine's stocks of Patriots have been depleted as Russia has escalated its ballistic missile campaign against the capital.

stories.headline: Update: Italy Suspends Schengen Rights for Spain as Ceuta Migrant Crisis Deepens
stories.summary:
Italy imposed air and sea border checks on Spain and temporarily suspended Spain's Schengen free-movement rights on Friday, citing the mass influx of an estimated 60,000 migrants who crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called scenes in Ceuta "shocking" as she announced the emergency measure, marking a significant fracture within the European Union over migration policy.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez condemned the Italian response as "selfish, polarizing and unlawful," insisting the integrity of the Schengen area remained guaranteed. Spanish authorities reported that most of the migrants had returned voluntarily to Morocco amid severe shortages of food, water and shelter in the tiny enclave, though thousands remained. At least 67 people died attempting the crossing, officials said.

The crisis has placed Sánchez in a politically exposed position. He has been among the most progressive European leaders on migration, and critics argue his stance left Spain unprepared for an event the president of Ceuta described as an overwhelming flood of arrivals since Thursday. Spain has deployed troops and resources to manage the situation.

The episode reopens deep divisions within the EU over burden-sharing and border enforcement. Italy's unilateral suspension of Schengen obligations for a fellow member state is legally contested and signals the fragility of European cohesion on migration, a pressure point that has fueled the rise of right-wing parties across the continent.

stories.headline: Independent Experts Confirm Pellet-Gun Wounds Among India Protest Crackdown Victims
stories.summary:
Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by at least four supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) during a large protest in New Delhi on July 20 are consistent with pellet-gun fire from security forces. The Indian government has not confirmed media reports that pellet guns were deployed during the crackdown, in which tens of thousands of protesters marched toward parliament to demand education reforms and the resignation of the education minister.

UK-based ballistics forensic scientist Philip Boyce told the BBC the injuries — dozens of tiny round punctures — were "definitely from a pellet gun," specifically a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, fired from at least 50 feet. Armament Research Services director NR Jenzen-Jones separately confirmed that images from the protests showed police using shotguns and that the injuries were "strongly consistent with the use of birdshot."

Delhi Police officially reported 60 protesters and 118 police personnel were injured during the crackdown, in which officers used wooden sticks, batons and tear gas on crowds. The CJP said the true number of injured protesters was substantially higher than the official count. A senior hospital official confirmed a fourth patient received treatment for pellet wounds.

The findings are significant because pellet guns, while used in crowd control in some countries, are banned in several others and are known to cause serious and occasionally life-threatening injuries, as well as toxic lead contamination. The BBC's investigation adds independent evidentiary weight to accounts that security forces used more severe measures than officially acknowledged against demonstrators seeking political accountability.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Declares Anti-Weaponization Fund 'Dead' as Blanche AG Nomination Remains Blocked
stories.summary:
President Trump told reporters at Camp David on Friday that his proposed $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund is 'dead,' saying administration officials had 'agreed not to have a fund' to compensate political allies — while simultaneously expressing personal disagreement with that decision. The contradictory statements came hours after Trump posted on social media defending compensation for those prosecuted in connection with the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, whom he described as 'suffering still, many ruined.'

The standoff centers on Todd Blanche's nomination as attorney general. Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina have refused to support Blanche until they receive written assurance the fund will not be created. Both senators said Trump's Friday comments made clear the fund remains 'still alive' in the president's mind, underscoring why they are demanding formal documentation. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley rescheduled a committee confirmation vote for Tuesday, saying he wants Blanche confirmed before the August recess.

The dispute highlights a rare intraparty clash within the Republican Senate caucus and the White House. Tillis, who is retiring, and Cornyn, who lost reelection after Trump backed his primary opponent, are negotiating from positions of relative independence. Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general throughout the impasse.

stories.headline: Update: Hundreds Evacuated by Sea as New Wildfires Break Out Across Greece; Europe Blazes Continue
stories.summary:
Around 500 people, mostly tourists, were stranded and evacuated by boat from the coastal town of Agios Vasileios in central Greece on Friday after a wildfire broke out and spread rapidly on strong winds. A second fire ignited further along the same coastline, while firefighters continued battling a large wildfire on Crete that has burned thousands of hectares and prompted the temporary evacuation of approximately 8,000 people. Fires have also broken out on the Greek islands of Paros, Andros, and Kalymnos.

The Greek blazes are part of a broader European wildfire crisis. Spain has seen more than 200,000 hectares burn in 2026 — roughly five times above the historical average for this point in the year — including what officials are calling the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history. Portugal, France, and Turkey are also battling active fires, with a new heatwave this week raising the risk of reignition near Madrid.

Climate scientists note that a mild, wet winter encouraged dense vegetation growth that subsequently dried out in successive heat waves, creating extreme fuel conditions. EU data shows burnt land across the continent is running well above historical norms. This story updates previous coverage of European wildfires; the new development is a fresh wave of evacuations in central mainland Greece and the confirmed sea evacuation of hundreds of tourists.

stories.headline: Harris Endorses Electoral College Abolition, Court Expansion at Urban League Speech
stories.summary:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris publicly backed abolishing the Electoral College and expanding the Supreme Court to 13 justices on Friday, positions she did not campaign on during her 2024 presidential run. Speaking at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville, Harris also suggested revisiting statehood for Puerto Rico, going beyond her prior support for Washington, D.C. statehood. 'We need to revisit the Electoral College,' Harris told the audience, acknowledging the remarks would be 'controversial coming from me, in particular' — a reference to her 2024 loss to Donald Trump in both the Electoral College and the popular vote.

Harris said she has not yet decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028, telling attendees she is 'fully, sincerely, focused on the midterms.' Multiple Democratic aides and strategists have publicly described her as the leading contender for the party's 2028 nomination. The speech came as reports indicated Harris has been reaching out to progressive groups, including pro-Palestinian organizations and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, signaling an effort to consolidate support on the party's left flank.

The policy shifts drew immediate reaction along partisan lines. Supporters see the positions as overdue democratic reforms; critics, including Republican commentators, argued that abolishing the Electoral College would fundamentally alter the constitutional balance between populous and less-populous states, and that court expansion would politicize the judiciary. The court-expansion proposal has previously been opposed by some moderate Democrats as well.

stories.headline: Update: Search Expands for Seven Missing Climbers on Pakistan's Broad Peak, Including Nirmal Purja
stories.summary:
Rescue teams entered a second day of searching Saturday for seven climbers still missing after a deadly avalanche struck a multinational expedition on Broad Peak, the world's 12th-highest mountain on the Pakistan-China border. Pakistani officials confirmed three bodies have been recovered and identified: American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy of Oman, and Pur Bahadur Gurung of Nepal. Among the seven still unaccounted for is Nirmal Purja, the renowned Nepali-British climber famous for summiting all 14 of the world's 8,000-meter peaks in just over six months in 2019.

The search operation has expanded to include local Pakistani climbers and Nepali mountaineers who halted their own expeditions on nearby K2. Drones have spotted several climbers on the mountain, but their condition remains unknown. Bad weather and the risk of further avalanches are hampering both helicopter and ground rescue efforts; military helicopters remain on standby pending improved conditions.

The avalanche struck the 8,047-meter peak on Thursday. Purja, a former British Special Boat Service operator, was leading the multinational expedition. The update from previous coverage is the confirmation of three named fatalities and the expanded multinational rescue operation now under way.
